Citrus and Bullets

By: Joy Summers | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
An orange farm in the Tugela valley becomes a batteground for warring factions, millions in invest is lost as government wakes up too late to the unfolding tragdey

Unique Selling Point:
ROLE PLAYERS PREPARED TO TELL THEIR STORY - FITS THE BILL PERFECTLY OF THE CARTE BLANCHE FORMULA: STRONG NARRATIVE BACKED BY THE BIGGER PICTURE OF THE NEED FOR INVESTMENT AND JOBS. WHILE RAMAPHOSA SPEAKS OF INVESTMENT - HERE WHERE THE RUBBER HITS THE ROAD WHERE THERE IS INVESTMENT - GOVERNMENT CANNOT PROVIDE ADEQUATE SAFETY AND SECURITY FOR THE INVESTMENT AND THE LIVES OF THOSE WHO DEPEND ON IT, TO FLOURISH.

Summary:
In 2017 a report was written on the land reform projects in the greater Weenen area of KZN. It covers an area of 83 000 hectares of land reform projects and all of them have failed following land transfer. Now, Sun Valley, a citrus farm in the Tugela Valley is the last jewel in the area and it too, is on its knees. And its violence and state ineptitude that put it there.


Further information:
Kobus Beukes is packing up his home and his family and moving out of the Tugela Valley. As general manager of Sun Valley the shooting and threats had become too much for him and his family. For the last few months he says his kids couldn’t even play outside and bodies were left to rot in the orchards.

He says he had been warning for months that the company that has invested over R100 million rand was on the verge of leaving. One more violent incident and he would go.

Then on Saturday the 28th September, he says he pushed the button and evacuated within 12 hours. Most of the moveable assets have also been removed. Ironically a peace agreement brokered by the Department of Security and Liaison. It was signed on the Monday after Kobus Beukes drove out of the valley for the last time, but it was too late.

Now the future of the only land reform project still working in the area hangs by a thread.

Workers are working in November with no guarantee they will get paid at the end of the month, the local agronomist who sprays the fruit has a vested interest in keeping the farm going and has been assisting where he can. But every- body is working on faith and hope, but the chances of an export crop of oranges in 2020 become slimmer as each day goes by.

The farm urgently needs a R12 million- rand investment and without that it will fail, and considering the events of the past few months, investors are quite literally gun shy.
The trees are planted on communal land and are still viable. But for how long?

Even the Premier of the Province has been roped in and actively involved in ensuring the peace process holds but as local farmer Roland Henderson says – they did nothing until it became a crisis.

So what went wrong? This year Sun Valley Farm produced 8.5 tonnes of navel oranges, valencia’s lemons and grapes, and there were plans for expansion. But all that came to a halt as the Citrus farm became a battle between two warring families.

The disagreements were between the KwaMadondo and Nhlawe communities but there were only two families within these communities at war. The Mthethwan’s and the Zungu’s. And the conflict ended in murders as a reign of terror spread across the valley for several months. The local police were both under resourced and scared to tackle men with AK 47’s and darkness in their hearts.

The source of the conflict is complicated but it’s a fight for resources, and while land is part of the problem it’s not the only problem. Fights over taxi routes in Johannesburg are brought home here to KZN and scores are settled.

Sun Valley was established in 1995 and was bought by the South African government in 2010 and given to the Silinkdokhule Trust which presently holds 9500 hectares of land. And the land restitution committee must also shoulder some responsibility. They just lumped 800 families and 9500 hectares of land into a single trust with nothing to bind them, and that has been a constant source of friction. Now the plan is to unbundle the trust but that is a long drawn out legal process that is still underway.

In the meantime Sun Valley, situated right between the two factions, became the battle ground. At times bullets flew and people were too scared to go to work. Now ACG fruit who have turned the farm into a profitable business for the last three years, say its safety first and they have removed their staff.

Enter Beef farmer Roland Henderson who is working with a government team and desperately in search of investors. Henderson is a straight- talking man and while he is trying to save the farm and convince investors – he is skeptical of government- “ they only stay for the photo opportunity and then leave’ he says.For now the security situation has improved and some arrests have been made.

Henderson says he has spoken to all the senior Induna’s in the area ( we can speak to them too) and they want Sun Valley to work. But nature waits for no man and if the oranges are to be accepted in Europe they must be sprayed for black spot now and there is no money for fertilizer. Its mission critical here at Sun Valley who without outside assistance will close within weeks.

Script:


Citrus and Bullets Final script TX 24th November 2019 for mix /2

Commentary One
This is the Inkosi Langalibalele district in KZN. It stretches from the Tugela river east of Weenen, to the foothills of the Drakensburg

What this impoverished region needs more than anything is investment and stability. But for the last 18 months a violent war between two families, the Madondo’s and Nhlawe’s has instead, chased investment away and left a reported 40 people murdered

Link
Violence is not new to this area, but the brutality of it shocked the locals, as women, children, herdsmen- people who had nothing to do with the disputes, were gunned down.

Commentary two
Now, the largest land redistribution project in the area - the Sun Valley Citrus estate could soon become another casualty of that violence.

Mac driving

I am on my way there, to find out why this once successful farm, owned by three local communities, and leased to an investor, could close within weeks

Car crosses river

Ample water and heat make Sun Valleys export quality oranges and grapes a profitable business. Turnover about R60 million with profits north of R10 million annually.

Roland Henderson
This is the last jewel in the crown as it were, Sun Valley

Commentary three
Roland Henderson is a beef farmer, and a member of the local district land reform committee. He has done in depth research into the farm

Roland
This farm is the largest agricultural employer in the whole of Inkosi Langalibaleli municipality. And it’s definitely the biggest in the Weenen area so peak season 700 people are employed, so for this to fail would be devastating to this particular area

BONGANI OPENS FARM DOOR

Commentary four
Bongani Madondo is Sun Valley’s production manager, and he’s working alongside Roland Henderson to save the farm.


Bongani
The community must come together, and they must understand that this is like a gold mine

Commentary Five
He has lost a family member to the violence, but he is cautious about what he says
Mac
Do we know who it was that was fighting?
Bongani Madondo
My brother, I don’t want to put myself at risk by pointing fingers at who may be involved in this.

Commentary six
His caution is understandable, although the killings happened outside the farm, a woman’s body was found in the orchard

Shots

Commentary seven
The net result of the violence was that people couldn’t get to work, harvests were late, and the investors began losing money

Roland:
it got to a point where the boundaries which were always respected in the past, in other words- you never attack women and children, you never attack businesses, you never attack farms and farmers, those boundaries became blurred, and it was because there wasn’t sufficient authority over the criminal elements or the tribal warfare. That then led to them essentially having a free for all across the area.

Commentary eight
Women slept in the bush. Walking to work could be deadly. These are the weapons, 74 in all, including high caliber rifles that have been confiscated by the police in the Weenen area over the last ten months.

Mpume Madondo is on the workers committee

Mpume
What we do, is that at around 6pm we make sure everyone is inside sleeping, because once it gets dark it’s not safe. You hear gunshots and you don’t know who it is, or what is going on

Commentary nine
The obvious question is what caused the fighting in the first place? But it was hard to get a straight answer. The farm is part of a trust, called Silindokuhle. Nkosingiphile Sibisi is one of the trustees.



Sibisi
No, when it comes to the fighting, I don’t know who is being beaten, who is hitting whom, and I don’t know the reason.

Commentary ten
Even Bheki Ntuli, the new MEC of the department of community safety and liaison doesn’t seem to know why.

Macfarlane
MEC in the conversations that you have had with the Induna or community, what sparked the fighting, and why were there so many killings?
Bheki Ntuli
You know here in KZN, you don’t have to have sound reasons why people would fight.

Commentary eleven
The reasons, according to several sources, began over taxi wars in Johannesburg which came home to this rural district. Then came the notorious hit men. The Izinkabi

MEC Beki Ntuli
Our province is very volatile in the sense that if there are taxi people fighting they would get Izinkabi from different areas to come and assist
Macfarlane
The issue of inkabi in KZN is huge, and it’s one that seems to be getting out of hand?
MEC
Ja not only in KZN, in the whole country.

Commentary twelve
I also met with several of the local induna at Sun Valley. I asked induna enkulu Mvelase leader of the Thembu tribe. He blames criminality and hitmen

INDUNA MVELASE
When we talk to the leaders here about what causes the violence, its mainly because of criminality and hitmen, and young people who are committing crime. Usually it’s because they don’t have money so they rob people, more than it’s about any faction fights. Just a lot of criminality that has increased

Commentary thirteen
In the Weenen area 52 000 hectares of farmland has been transferred to 11 community trusts. The outcome has been disastrous for most of them, and Sun Valley is no different.
Here three communities own the land, but nine different communities made up the Silindokhule trust. And they all want their share of the resource

Macfarlane
For you, you feel this arrangement was forced upon the community?
Sibisi
Yes, they were forced to be part of this.
Macfarlane
What do you think would resolve this?
Sibisi
According to us, the department should have given the community the title deed so they can stand alone and manage their own land, trust by trust.

LINK
Eventually the warring families signed a peace agreement, but it came just too late. Only three days earlier the investors had had enough, and drove away with all the moveable assets.

Commentary fourteen
The investors, ACG fruit had pumped millions into the farm, and late in September they cleaned out their offices, and quietly left within 12 hours. In their response to us they say:

“What happened at Sun Valley is indeed sad or rather tragic. So many good people are now suffering and therefore we view it would be inappropriate and even insensitive to get involved in a debate in the public domain.”debate

Macfarlane
When you look at the peace agreement and the conversations that Induna are having, do you think it’s a little bit too late?
Bongani
Yes I would say it’s very late, if you are talking about 40 people it’s very late

Commentary Fifteen
The police say they have ongoing operations in the area. But the violence happened at night and that is when the local police needed to respond. Mpume Madondo says they don’t

Mpume Madondo
The police here don’t help us. When you call them they tell you directly we are scared of that place, that community. So they don’t help us with anything, in fact they are the ones who make us lose a lot of hope, to the extent that we don’t feel safe because even the law enforcers tell you straight, that you are not safe, that they are scared.
How can we keep safe when the law enforcers themselves can’t help us? They are the ones who should help us, that we need close to us. And right now as the situation is, here at Sun Valley, they haven’t come to help us at all.

Mac
Speaking to some of the villagers, they felt that they had been let down by the police…
MEC Bheki Ntuli
They may say that because they are stressful, but let me tell you these firearms that were recovered were recovered by the police, so it may not necessarily be true.
Macfarlane
Do you have any indication of how many arrests have been made?
MEC Bheki Ntuli
From April to date, there were 33 arrests, but we do know that some may not be found guilty, because the justice system has got its own way of working


Commentary sixteen
Induna enkula Mvelase says he wants to see Sun Valley expand

Macfarlane
Sir, why did it take so long to meet to find a solution for what is happening here?
INDUNA
When you are dealing with crime, and people are benefitting, and you are trying to stop the whole thing- so then they ask themselves how are we going to benefit? So they create a diversion, so that is no longer a fight, its now criminality, and that is why it took such a long time to stop it.

Commentary seventeen
Now its mission critical down here on the farm.

Link
R12 million rand is needed within weeks or the farm will close, and local farmers, and the workers are all chipping in to save it.

Commentary eighteen
Henderson has been knocking on government doors, hoping for R12 million in emergency funds, giving them time to find a new investor.

Macfarlane
Seven hundred jobs are at stake, 40 people murdered. Is the premier even listening?
Roland Henderson
No the premier is. However the wheels of government move slowly and they move far too slowly for an operation such as this

Commentary nineteen
Farming basically stopped in October, but they need to spray the oranges now, to ensure access to export markets next year

Roland
So its exceptionally time sensitive we are running out of time day by day to resurrect the farm and have an export crop

Commentary twenty
Meanwhile the local agronomist, farmers and some workers are all lending a free hand, hoping for a miracle.

Thandeka Shezi is a quality controller during picking

Thandeka
Now that the employment has ended, I am not all right because even at home I am the sole provider.


Bongani
The situation is very terrible it’s not good, our heart is sore, because we are not working, you know that next year January that some of the parents ….it’s only one place that they know that they can get money to take their kids to school.

Commentary twenty- one
Zinhle Dladla is a pruner

Zinhle Dladla
It’s really painful, because I have one child and when I ran out of something I was able to buy it at any time, I didn’t have to wait for the child grant.
MAC
So it’s important for things to be resolved here?
Zinhle
We would be really happy if help could come, so this company could be on its feet again.

Commentary twenty- two
There IS a small ray of hope for Sun Valley. Right now the peace agreement is holding and it will be sealed with a cleansing ceremony next month.

Roland
The agreement will hold if there is more work behind it – in other words the families must honour the agreement, they must complete the ceremonies which are needed to cleanse the air as it were, the Induna who are responsible for making that happen are totally committed to doing that . So it will hold, but it needs a lot of work, it won’t hold just because the peace of paper was signed

Commentary Twenty- three
Tomorrow the Land Bank will visit the farm. Now police, and safety and liaison must play their part if there is any hope of fulfilling the presidents promise of investment, job creation and a growing economy

Bongani
If there is anyone who is willing to open this place, we would welcome them with open arms, just to make it function once again.

THE END 11 56










PROMO ONE
Violence between two families in the Weenen area has spilled over onto a profitable community owned citrus farm. The investor has fled and now the farms future hangs in the balance

PROMO TWO
Since January this year police in the Weenen area have confiscated 74 illegal firearms after a murderous killing spree that could close the only export citrus farm in the area.

PROMO THREE
A community citrus farm, close to the Tugela river, has been blighted by violence. Now the race is on to save it
Roland
we are running out of time day by day to resurrect the farm and have an export crop

Macfarlane MEC in the conversations that you have had with the Induna or community, what sparked the fighting, and why were there so many killings? Bheki Ntuli You know here in KZN, you don’t have to have sound reasons why people would fight. Commentary eleven The reasons, according to several sources, began over taxi wars in Johannesburg which came home to this rural district. Then came the notorious hit men. The Izinkabi MEC Beki Ntuli Our province is very volatile in the sense that if there are taxi people fighting they would get Izinkabi from different areas to come and assist Macfarlane The issue of inkabi in KZN is huge, and it’s one that seems to be getting out of hand? MEC Ja not only in KZN, in the whole country. Commentary twelve I also met with several of the local induna at Sun Valley. I asked induna enkulu Mvelase leader of the Thembu tribe. He blames criminality and hitmen INDUNA MVELASE When we talk to the leaders here about what causes the violence, its mainly because of criminality and hitmen, and young people who are committing crime. Usually it’s because they don’t have money so they rob people, more than it’s about any faction fights. Just a lot of criminality that has increased Commentary thirteen In the Weenen area 52 000 hectares of farmland has been transferred to 11 community trusts. The outcome has been disastrous for most of them, and Sun Valley is no different. Here three communities own the land, but nine different communities made up the Silindokhule trust. And they all want their share of the resource Macfarlane For you, you feel this arrangement was forced upon the community? Sibisi Yes, they were forced to be part of this. Macfarlane What do you think would resolve this? Sibisi According to us, the department should have given the community the title deed so they can stand alone and manage their own land, trust by trust. LINK Eventually the warring families signed a peace agreement, but it came just too late. Only three days earlier the investors had had enough, and drove away with all the moveable assets. Commentary fourteen The investors, ACG fruit had pumped millions into the farm, and late in September they cleaned out their offices, and quietly left within 12 hours. In their response to us they say: “What happened at Sun Valley is indeed sad or rather tragic. So many good people are now suffering and therefore we view it would be inappropriate and even insensitive to get involved in a debate in the public domain.”debate Macfarlane When you look at the peace agreement and the conversations that Induna are having, do you think it’s a little bit too late? Bongani Yes I would say it’s very late, if you are talking about 40 people it’s very late Commentary Fifteen The police say they have ongoing operations in the area. But the violence happened at night and that is when the local police needed to respond. Mpume Madondo says they don’t Mpume Madondo The police here don’t help us. When you call them they tell you directly we are scared of that place, that community. So they don’t help us with anything, in fact they are the ones who make us lose a lot of hope, to the extent that we don’t feel safe because even the law enforcers tell you straight, that you are not safe, that they are scared. How can we keep safe when the law enforcers themselves can’t help us? They are the ones who should help us, that we need close to us. And right now as the situation is, here at Sun Valley, they haven’t come to help us at all. Mac Speaking to some of the villagers, they felt that they had been let down by the police… MEC Bheki Ntuli They may say that because they are stressful, but let me tell you these firearms that were recovered were recovered by the police, so it may not necessarily be true. Macfarlane Do you have any indication of how many arrests have been made? MEC Bheki Ntuli From April to date, there were 33 arrests, but we do know that some may not be found guilty, because the justice system has got its own way of working Commentary sixteen Induna enkula Mvelase says he wants to see Sun Valley expand Macfarlane Sir, why did it take so long to meet to find a solution for what is happening here? INDUNA When you are dealing with crime, and people are benefitting, and you are trying to stop the whole thing- so then they ask themselves how are we going to benefit? So they create a diversion, so that is no longer a fight, its now criminality, and that is why it took such a long time to stop it. Commentary seventeen Now its mission critical down here on the farm. Link R12 million rand is needed within weeks or the farm will close, and local farmers, and the workers are all chipping in to save it. Commentary eighteen Henderson has been knocking on government doors, hoping for R12 million in emergency funds, giving them time to find a new investor. Macfarlane Seven hundred jobs are at stake, 40 people murdered. Is the premier even listening? Roland Henderson No the premier is. However the wheels of government move slowly and they move far too slowly for an operation such as this Commentary nineteen Farming basically stopped in October, but they need to spray the oranges now, to ensure access to export markets next year Roland So its exceptionally time sensitive we are running out of time day by day to resurrect the farm and have an export crop Commentary twenty Meanwhile the local agronomist, farmers and some workers are all lending a free hand, hoping for a miracle. Thandeka Shezi is a quality controller during picking Thandeka Now that the employment has ended, I am not all right because even at home I am the sole provider. Bongani The situation is very terrible it’s not good, our heart is sore, because we are not working, you know that next year January that some of the parents ….it’s only one place that they know that they can get money to take their kids to school. Commentary twenty- one Zinhle Dladla is a pruner Zinhle Dladla It’s really painful, because I have one child and when I ran out of something I was able to buy it at any time, I didn’t have to wait for the child grant. MAC So it’s important for things to be resolved here? Zinhle We would be really happy if help could come, so this company could be on its feet again. Commentary twenty- two There IS a small ray of hope for Sun Valley. Right now the peace agreement is holding and it will be sealed with a cleansing ceremony next month. Roland The agreement will hold if there is more work behind it – in other words the families must honour the agreement, they must complete the ceremonies which are needed to cleanse the air as it were, the Induna who are responsible for making that happen are totally committed to doing that . So it will hold, but it needs a lot of work, it won’t hold just because the peace of paper was signed Commentary Twenty- three Tomorrow the Land Bank will visit the farm. Now police, and safety and liaison must play their part if there is any hope of fulfilling the presidents promise of investment, job creation and a growing economy Bongani If there is anyone who is willing to open this place, we would welcome them with open arms, just to make it function once again. THE END 11 56 PROMO ONE Violence between two families in the Weenen area has spilled over onto a profitable community owned citrus farm. The investor has fled and now the farms future hangs in the balance PROMO TWO Since January this year police in the Weenen area have confiscated 74 illegal firearms after a murderous killing spree that could close the only export citrus farm in the area. PROMO THREE A community citrus farm, close to the Tugela river, has been blighted by violence. Now the race is on to save it Roland we are running out of time day by day to resurrect the farm and have an export crop Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for Citrus and Bullets (5579) Joy Summers 27 November 2019

metadata.Summary: In 2017 a report was written on the land reform projects in the greater Weenen area of KZN. It covers an area of 83 000 hectares of land reform projects and all of them have failed following land transfer. Now, Sun Valley, a citrus farm in the Tugela Valley is the last jewel in the area and it too, is on its knees. And its violence and state ineptitude that put it there.
metadata.Further information: Kobus Beukes is packing up his home and his family and moving out of the Tugela Valley. As general manager of Sun Valley the shooting and threats had become too much for him and his family. For the last few months he says his kids couldn’t even play outside and bodies were left to rot in the orchards. He says he had been warning for months that the company that has invested over R100 million rand was on the verge of leaving. One more violent incident and he would go. Then on Saturday the 28th September, he says he pushed the button and evacuated within 12 hours. Most of the moveable assets have also been removed. Ironically a peace agreement brokered by the Department of Security and Liaison. It was signed on the Monday after Kobus Beukes drove out of the valley for the last time, but it was too late. Now the future of the only land reform project still working in the area hangs by a thread. Workers are working in November with no guarantee they will get paid at the end of the month, the local agronomist who sprays the fruit has a vested interest in keeping the farm going and has been assisting where he can. But every- body is working on faith and hope, but the chances of an export crop of oranges in 2020 become slimmer as each day goes by. The farm urgently needs a R12 million- rand investment and without that it will fail, and considering the events of the past few months, investors are quite literally gun shy. The trees are planted on communal land and are still viable. But for how long? Even the Premier of the Province has been roped in and actively involved in ensuring the peace process holds but as local farmer Roland Henderson says – they did nothing until it became a crisis. So what went wrong? This year Sun Valley Farm produced 8.5 tonnes of navel oranges, valencia’s lemons and grapes, and there were plans for expansion. But all that came to a halt as the Citrus farm became a battle between two warring families. The disagreements were between the KwaMadondo and Nhlawe communities but there were only two families within these communities at war. The Mthethwan’s and the Zungu’s. And the conflict ended in murders as a reign of terror spread across the valley for several months. The local police were both under resourced and scared to tackle men with AK 47’s and darkness in their hearts. The source of the conflict is complicated but it’s a fight for resources, and while land is part of the problem it’s not the only problem. Fights over taxi routes in Johannesburg are brought home here to KZN and scores are settled. Sun Valley was established in 1995 and was bought by the South African government in 2010 and given to the Silinkdokhule Trust which presently holds 9500 hectares of land. And the land restitution committee must also shoulder some responsibility. They just lumped 800 families and 9500 hectares of land into a single trust with nothing to bind them, and that has been a constant source of friction. Now the plan is to unbundle the trust but that is a long drawn out legal process that is still underway. In the meantime Sun Valley, situated right between the two factions, became the battle ground. At times bullets flew and people were too scared to go to work. Now ACG fruit who have turned the farm into a profitable business for the last three years, say its safety first and they have removed their staff. Enter Beef farmer Roland Henderson who is working with a government team and desperately in search of investors. Henderson is a straight- talking man and while he is trying to save the farm and convince investors – he is skeptical of government- “ they only stay for the photo opportunity and then leave’ he says.For now the security situation has improved and some arrests have been made. Henderson says he has spoken to all the senior Induna’s in the area ( we can speak to them too) and they want Sun Valley to work. But nature waits for no man and if the oranges are to be accepted in Europe they must be sprayed for black spot now and there is no money for fertilizer. Its mission critical here at Sun Valley who without outside assistance will close within weeks.
